timelineEvents.title: Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.label: 1935 · Hollywood debut
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper makes his Hollywood debut at MGM, contributing to Escapade and other major studio projects.
timelineEvents.longDescription: First American score: "Escapade" (dir. Robert Z. Leonard) with William Powell and Luise Rainer. Press hails "Two New Composers" of Kiepura's European hits. Songs also for Marx Brothers' "A Night at the Opera" (with Ned Washington) and "Mutiny on the Bounty".

timelineEvents.title: Continued success
timelineEvents.label: 1937 · Continued Hollywood success
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper continues his Hollywood success with MGM musicals and new lyricist collaborations.
timelineEvents.longDescription: "Everybody Sing" with "Melody Farm" and "The One I Love"; collaborations with Gus Kahn and Paul Francis Webster.

timelineEvents.title: New chapter
timelineEvents.label: 1939 · Solo MGM chapter begins
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper remains at MGM and begins a new solo chapter as a film composer.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper remains with MGM, starting a solo career as a film composer.

timelineEvents.title: MGM markets Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers”
timelineEvents.label: MGM’s “Viennese” label
timelineEvents.shortDescription: American studio publicity recast Kaper and Jurmann as a Viennese composing team, turning “Vienna” into a promotional brand rather than a biographical fact.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Soon after their arrival at MGM, the American press and studio publicity presented Kaper and Jurmann as “Viennese composers” and as a brilliant Viennese musical team. The label suited MGM’s first use of the duo in Escapade, a Hollywood remake of the Viennese film Maskerade, but it was biographically misleading for Kaper, whose career had developed in Warsaw and Berlin. The event marks the moment when Hollywood began to translate his European professional history into a marketable studio identity.
